title: Maldives Joins Bangladesh in Pushing for SAARC Revival as Muizzu Offers to Bridge India-Pakistan Divide
excerpt: President Muizzu used the Maldives' Independence Day address to call on South Asian nations to resume dialogue, with the regional bloc dormant since 2016.
body:
• Maldives President Mohamed Muizzu called for reviving SAARC during the country's 61st Independence Day celebrations, offering to play a constructive role in restarting dialogue.
  • Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman reinforced the message during a meeting with Muizzu in Malé, with both sides stressing the need to "reinvigorate" the regional bloc.
  • SAARC has been effectively frozen since 2016, when India pulled out of an Islamabad summit after a militant attack it blamed on Pakistan.
  • India has since shifted its regional cooperation focus to BIMSTEC, which includes most SAARC members but excludes Pakistan.

Muizzu's Push

Maldives President Mohamed Muizzu used his address during the country's 61st Independence Day celebrations to renew calls for reviving the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, urging member nations to overcome differences through dialogue.

"Both sides "underscored the importance of reinvigorating SAARC," according to a press release."

"South Asia would benefit from stronger collaboration," Muizzu told diplomats and representatives from several countries and international organisations in Malé. He said the Maldives was prepared to play a constructive role in helping member nations restart talks and bridge existing differences.

Bangladesh Adds Its Voice

The call gained momentum when Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman, visiting Malé as a special guest for the Independence Day celebrations, met Muizzu at the President's Office on July 25. Both sides "underscored the importance of reinvigorating SAARC," according to a press release.

Bangladesh has been the most vocal advocate for SAARC revival in recent months. Consultations are reportedly underway with member states about convening a meeting of senior officials and exploring a special session of the Council of Ministers to restart the regional platform. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's government has made SAARC revival a diplomatic priority.

Why SAARC Stalled

SAARC — which comprises Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka — has been largely dormant since 2016. The planned Islamabad summit that year was indefinitely postponed after India withdrew following a militant attack on an Indian Army base at Uri in Kashmir, which New Delhi blamed on Pakistan-based groups. Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Bhutan followed India's lead.

Since then, India has channelled its regional cooperation efforts through BIMSTEC (Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation), which includes most SAARC members but notably excludes Pakistan. Critics of this approach argue that excluding the region's second-largest economy limits the potential for South Asian economic integration.

India's Calculus

New Delhi has shown little appetite for reviving SAARC in its current form. India's position has consistently been that Pakistan's support for cross-border terrorism makes meaningful cooperation impossible within the SAARC framework. The brief thaw in India-Pakistan relations in January — when External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar attended former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Khaleda Zia's funeral alongside Pakistan's National Assembly Speaker — has not translated into a shift on SAARC.

For the South Asian diaspora — spanning millions across the Gulf, Europe and North America — SAARC revival holds symbolic and practical significance. A functional regional bloc could ease trade barriers, simplify travel and strengthen cultural ties across a region that remains among the world's least integrated economically despite deep historical connections.
nri_angle: SAARC revival could reshape trade, travel and cultural ties across South Asia, directly affecting diaspora communities from all eight member nations.
